posts.title: The chestnut loaf is back for autumn
posts.excerpt: Roasted chestnuts folded into a rye sourdough, one tray a day until the first frost. Here is how Emi bakes it.
posts.content:
Every October the first box of chestnuts arrives from the Oda farm, still in their spiky shells. That is the signal: the chestnut loaf is back on the board.

Roasted, peeled, folded in

Taro roasts the chestnuts in the morning oven while it cools down, peels them by hand and breaks them into rough pieces. They go into a rye and wheat sourdough at the last fold, so they stay whole and sweet in the crumb.

It is the loaf people ask about in August. We make them wait.

Emi Nakano, head baker

There is one tray a day, so reserve yours if you can. It keeps well for four days wrapped in a cloth, and it toasts beautifully with salted butter.

posts.title: Twenty-seven layers: how a croissant is folded
posts.excerpt: Butter, a cold room and three folds. Taro explains why our croissants take two days and shatter the way they do.
posts.content:
A croissant is mostly patience. The dough is mixed in the afternoon, rested overnight, then wrapped around a sheet of cold cultured butter the next morning.

Three folds, three rests

Each fold triples the layers: three, then nine, then twenty-seven. Between folds the dough rests in the cold room, so the butter stays firm and the layers stay apart.

  1. Roll the dough around the butter and fold it in three.
  2. Rest it cold for forty minutes, then turn and fold again.
  3. Repeat once more, rest overnight, then roll, cut and shape.

In the oven the water in the butter turns to steam and lifts every layer. That is the shattering you hear when you bite into one.

posts.title: French toast from day-old shokupan
posts.excerpt: A slice two fingers thick, a simple custard and a warm skillet: Saki's weekend breakfast for the end of the milk loaf.
posts.content:
Milk bread is at its softest on the first day. On the second it is perfect for French toast: firm enough to soak up custard without falling apart.

For two thick slices

  • 2 slices of shokupan, about 4 cm thick
  • 2 eggs and 150 ml milk
  • 1 tablespoon sugar and a pinch of salt
  • Butter for the pan

Whisk the eggs, milk, sugar and salt. Soak the slices for five minutes on each side. Melt butter in a pan over low heat, cook the slices with a lid on for six minutes, turn, and cook four more without the lid until golden.

Low heat and a lid. That is the whole secret.

Saki Mori, at the counter

posts.title: Ten years in the old rice shop
posts.excerpt: One secondhand oven, a bench with old scale marks and a street that kept coming back. A thank-you from all six of us.
posts.content:
Ten years ago we signed the lease on a narrow shop that had sold rice for three generations. The bench still had the merchant's scale marks. We kept it.

What has changed, and what has not

We are six now instead of two. We bake for four cafés and deliver by bicycle. But the oven is the same one, and Mr. Hoshino from across the road is still, most mornings, our first customer.

He buys one baguette and tells us the weather. Every day for ten years.

Emi Nakano

On the anniversary weekend every loaf comes with a small melon pan, and the children of the street get to stamp the paper bags. Thank you for ten warm years.

posts.title: Feeding a sourdough starter at home
posts.excerpt: Our levain is ten years old. Yours can start this week: flour, water, a jar and five days of attention.
posts.content:
A starter is just flour and water that have caught the wild yeasts around them. It needs feeding, warmth and a little patience.

Five days to a lively starter

  1. Day 1: mix 50 g wholemeal flour with 50 g water in a clean jar. Cover loosely.
  2. Days 2 to 4: discard half, then add 50 g flour and 50 g water each day.
  3. Day 5: when it doubles within six hours of feeding, it is ready to bake with.

Keep it on the kitchen counter if you bake often, or in the fridge with a weekly feed if you do not. Ask at the counter and we will give you a spoonful of ours to start.

posts.title: Melon pan for the school fair
posts.excerpt: Three hundred melon pan, forty small helpers and one very busy oven. Notes from the summer school fair.
posts.content:
Every summer the primary school down the street holds its fair, and every summer we bake melon pan for it. This year the children helped.

Forty pairs of small hands

Taro made the cookie dough the day before. On the morning of the fair, forty children pressed the crisscross pattern into the tops with wooden cards, very seriously, one bun at a time.

Some of them came out more like turtles than melons. Those sold first.

Taro Ishida, pastry

All three hundred were gone by noon. Thank you to the teachers, the parents and our youngest bakers.

products.name: Milk Shokupan
products.short: Tall, soft and milky, baked in a lidded tin. The bread for thick toast.
products.description:
Our most-loved loaf. Hokkaido-style milk bread made with a scalded flour paste (yudane), so the crumb stays cloud-soft and keeps for three days.

Ask for it sliced thick for toast or thin for sandwiches. On day two it makes the best French toast.

products.name: Country Sourdough
products.short: A three-day levain, a dark blistered crust and an open, tangy crumb.
products.description:
Flour, water, salt and our ten-year-old levain. The dough rests for a night and a day before it is baked dark on the oven stone.

Keep it cut side down on a board, wrapped in a cloth. It is still good on day five, toasted.

products.name: Morning Baguette
products.short: A thin, crackling crust over a creamy crumb. Baked twice a day.
products.description: A slow, cold-fermented baguette with a crackling crust and a creamy, open crumb. We bake it at dawn and again in the afternoon for dinner tables.

products.name: Stone-oven Batard
products.short: Rye and spelt with a little honey, baked straight on the oven stone.
products.description:
A sturdy oval loaf of rye, spelt and wheat with a spoonful of honey, baked directly on the stone for a thick, caramelised crust.

Lovely with cheese, soup or just butter and salt.

products.name: Butter Croissant
products.short: Cultured butter folded into twenty-seven layers, shattering at the edges.
products.description:
Two days in the making: an overnight dough, three folds of cold cultured butter and a slow final rise. It shatters at the edges and stays tender inside.

Warm it for three minutes in a hot oven if you eat it later in the day.

products.name: Cinnamon Roll
products.short: Cardamom dough rolled with cinnamon sugar, glazed while still warm.
products.description: A soft cardamom dough rolled with brown sugar and Ceylon cinnamon, baked until the edges caramelise and glazed at the counter while still warm.

products.name: Melon Pan
products.short: A crackled cookie crust over a soft milk bun. No melon, only joy.
products.description: A soft milk bun under a crisp, sugary cookie crust, pressed with the crisscross pattern that gives it its name. The children's favourite, and secretly ours too.

products.name: Sesame Anpan
products.short: Smooth red-bean paste in a soft bun under toasted sesame.
products.description: A soft, glazed bun filled with smooth red-bean paste that we cook ourselves from Hokkaido azuki, finished with toasted white sesame.
